157: Breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing and arbitrary or capricious performance evaluations: the court held the government did not breach the covenant and the evaluations were not arbitrary.
Accordingly, the Court of Federal Claims correctly determined the Government did not breach the covenant of good faith and fair dealing.
222: Type I differing site condition equitable adjustment: the Board's finding that the actual soil conditions were reasonably foreseeable to the contractor, defeating the claim.
Accordingly, we conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that the soil conditions were reasonably foreseeable to CCI.
223: Type I differing site condition equitable adjustment: the Board's finding that the contractor did not rely on the Andrea Report's site representations, defeating the claim.
In light of this evidence, we hold that a reasonable mind could conclude that CCI did not rely on the Andrea Report in preparing its proposal.
419: Negligent estimate recovery: Claims Court clearly erred in finding DRMS provided a realistic estimate under FAR 16.503 and no causal link; court reversed denial of the contractor's claim and remanded for calculation of equitable adjustment.
We reverse the Claims Court's denial of Agility's negligent estimate claim and remand for calculation of Agility's equitable adjustment.
420: Government's defense that scrap sales proceeds offset or limit the contractor's recovery was rejected; the contractor may retain scrap proceeds and still recover.
Under the parties' contract, however, Agility's receipt of scrap proceeds does not limit Agility's recovery.
439: Excusable default and government-caused default defenses: the court held the Navy's review of the replacement bonds did not excuse the default under 48 C.F.R. 52.249-10(b) because the contractor caused the default.
Because AECI has failed to establish any grounds for excusing its material breach or otherwise shifting liability to the Navy, the CFC’s decision to dismiss these claims is affirmed.
532: Quantum and equitable adjustment: whether the contractor was entitled to an equitable adjustment for increased fuel costs under the changes clause.
Accordingly, the increase in fuel prices was not a change to the contract triggering FAR § 52.243-4; the contract allocated to DG21 the risk of rising fuel prices.
684: Bid preparation and proposal costs recoverable under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(2) in a bid protest; contractor who never submitted or prepared a proposal cannot recover any costs
We agree with the CFC that IDEA is not entitled to recover any costs because IDEA did not submit or prepare a bid proposal.
1427: Constructive acceleration claim: contractor failed to show a denied or unacted-on request for time extension, so summary judgment for the government on the constructive change theory was affirmed

Because Zafer failed to designate specific facts sufficient to establish that USACE denied a request for a time extension, we affirm the Claims Court's conclusion that Zafer failed to establish a constructive acceleration claim.
1428: Government fault / sovereign acts theory of constructive change: the government was not responsible for the Pakistani route closure and negotiations were not specifically directed at nullifying contract rights, so summary judgment for the government was affirmed
First, the U.S. government was not responsible for the route closure. As both parties have acknowledged, the Pakistan government alone closed the route
1462: Recoverable damages for costs of loading spent nuclear fuel into storage casks caused by the government's partial breach; the court held the Court of Federal Claims clearly erred in denying these costs and reversed.

We agree with System Fuels that the Court of Federal Claims clearly erred in both decisions when it denied damages for costs incurred to load the storage casks and/or canisters, regardless of the type of fuel loaded.
1560: Government's prior material breach defense excusing its nonperformance of payment obligations; the court held Laguna's kickback-tainted vouchers were a first material breach, so the government's nonperformance was excused.

Accordingly, we affirm the Board's grant of the government's summary judgment motion on the grounds that Laguna's prior material breach of the Allowable Cost and Payment clause excused the government's nonperformance.
1561: Laguna's argument that the government waived the prior material breach defense through continued performance and payment after learning of the kickback scheme was rejected.
Therefore, the government did not waive its right to invoke the prior material breach rule.
1771: Government defense that it lacked authority to pay FTCA damages in periodic installments absent a statute. The court rejected the defense, holding periodic payments permissible by agreement of the parties.
The Government's persistence in this case—that no authority exists for paying damages in periodic installments—fails to account for circumstances where the parties expressly agree to such payments.
2153: Release as a contract defense to the breach of contract claim: the Court of Federal Claims held the release barred Ingham's claim; the Federal Circuit held the release in the same contract cannot bar a claim for breach of that contract.
Similarly here, the Release cannot be enforced against a claim for breach of the underlying contract.
2201: Quantum and damages: whether the contractor proved it was harmed and is entitled to contract damages after assigning its delivery order payments; summary judgment for the Government affirmed.
Northrop has not met its burden of establishing damages. The undisputed facts show that Northrop has suffered no harm.
2340: Quantum of lost-profit damages for breach of the HAP contract; the Claims Court reduced damages to zero because the contractor failed to prove saved costs and expenses with reasonable certainty, and the Federal Circuit affirmed.
Because Englewood failed to prove the expenses and costs savings element of its lost profits with reasonable certainty, the Claims Court was justified in awarding no damages.
2605: Contract defenses on the breach of contract claim: the contest's limitation-of-liability clause barred claims based on the judging process absent fraud, irregularity, intentional misconduct, gross mistake, or lack of good faith, so summary judgment for the government was affirmed.

Because Mr. Frankel is unable to show "fraud, irregularity, intentional misconduct, gross mistake, or lack of good faith involved in the contest," any other breach of contract claim based on the judging process is barred by the contest's limitation of liability clause.
2982: Recoverability of pre-litigation attorney fees for claim preparation under common law damages principles; court affirmed award for contractor.
We affirm the trial court's ruling that SUFI is entitled to attorney fees under common law.
2984: Reasonableness of attorneys' standard hourly rates used in the lodestar fee calculation; court found no clear error and affirmed the fee award.
We find no clear error in the trial court's award of fees based on SUFI's attorneys' standard rates.
2985: Recoverability of overhead and lost profit under common law rather than the FAR excessive pass-through rule; court held the FAR does not apply and vacated the denial.
Thus, we vacate the trial court's denial of overhead and profit and remand with instructions that the trial court apply law consistent with this opinion.
3106: Constructive acceleration claim rejected because the contractor never made a timely, formal request for a time extension that was denied; contractor's claim for additional damages fails.
Garco fails to make a prima facie case of constructive acceleration for an additional reason.
3810: Breach of paragraph 21 (premature termination): summary judgment for government because any breach would result in no damages given non-pay, non-duty status. Court found no error.
we find no error in the decision of the court concerning Ms. VanDesande's termination claim.
3811: Contract defense based on noncompliance with paragraph 29 certified-mail service requirement for the accountant's calculations. Court held the claimant substantially complied, so the government's defense failed, and awarded $33,691 in 2003 tax consequences.

We thus hold that the attachment of the accountant-prepared calculations to the motion for reconsideration constituted substantial compliance with the service requirement of paragraph 29 of the Stipulation Agreement.
3946: Quantum of contract damages under the Avgas Contracts: attribution of acid waste, pre-contract activity, acid sludge, non-contractual avgas, and reasonable certainty of damages
The Court of Federal Claims did not abuse its discretion by crediting the Stipulation and Parties' Statements to make its damages calculation through 1998.
4046: Quantum meruit recovery: the quantum meruit theory is essentially an implied-in-fact theory that cannot survive dismissal, so the quantum meruit claim was properly dismissed.
The trial court therefore properly dismissed the plaintiffs' quantum meruit claim as well.
4076: Denial of RDA's superior knowledge, cardinal change, differing site conditions and time extension claims for equitable adjustment and recovery, affirmed under the clear-error standard.
we may only reverse the judgment on appeal if we conclude that the Claims Court's findings were clearly erroneous.
4180: Type I differing site condition: contractor's entitlement to equitable adjustment for materially different subsurface conditions; reversal because contractor failed to prove reasonable reliance on its interpretation of the contract.
Because Grimberg was unreasonable, under long-established law, it is not entitled to an equitable adjustment of the contract price.
4544: Equitable adjustment: contractor failed to prove damages for the Sherwin Williams paint theory raised by the Board, so no recovery
A required element of a claim for equitable adjustment is proof of damages.
4546: Quantum for Baker design versus structural-brick design: contractor entitled to the full difference in construction costs, not only the design costs the Board awarded
We reverse the Board’s denial of recovery to Parsons for its claim to construction costs.
4547: Reasonableness of contractor's claimed costs; government's burden-shifting argument rejected and any error harmless
We affirm the Board’s conclusion that Parsons’ claimed costs were reasonable.
4902: Meadowbrook property: impossibility defense based on the City's stop-work order rejected because Halim was at fault for the order.
His plea of impossibility is therefore not a viable defense to liability on the contracts.
4903: Beacon Light property: mutual mistake defense rejected because Halim lacked due diligence and bore the risk of zoning restrictions.
Where the parties have allocated the risk of mistake to one of the parties, that party may not invoke the doctrine of mutual mistake to avoid its contractual obligations.
4904: Beacon Light property: impossibility defense based on the city's denial of a variance rejected because the risk was allocated to the purchaser.
Mr. Halim's impossibility argument fails on the same ground.
4938: Quantum/constructive change: whether a third-party Base expansion and resulting security changes entitle the contractor to equitable adjustment; no constructive change found, so no compensation.
Because the Board correctly concluded that the change in security procedures was not a constructive change in the contract for which ECC is entitled to compensation, we affirm.
5131: Government's contract defense that the Assistant U.S. Attorney lacked settlement authority to bind the government to payments exceeding $400,000, and that the agreement should be read to preserve enforceability; rejected.
This argument falls flat. As a preliminary matter, we discern no ambiguity regarding the government's payment obligations under the Settlement Agreement
5156: Allowability of contractor defense costs: the Tecom standard applies, so defense costs are allowable only if the underlying discrimination claims had very little likelihood of success, and the costs here are not allowable.
We conclude that the standard articulated in Tecom applies to the costs at issue here.
5962: Quantum: whether the government's disallowance of $253 million in post-retirement benefit costs was proper, given the Board's finding that Northrop never claimed and will never claim those costs (affirmed on substantial evidence).

We conclude that substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that Northrop's negative PRB plan amendment effectively eliminated Northrop's transition obligation. We therefore affirm the Board's decision that the government's disallowance of the disputed $253,361,512 of Northrop's PRB costs was improper
6070: Type I differing site conditions claim (Counts II and V): Court held no compensable differing site condition because the saturated soil was reasonably foreseeable, so no equitable adjustment was owed.
We cannot say that the Court of Federal Claims clearly erred in its determination that the subsurface soil conditions were reasonably foreseeable based on the Contract.
6072: Accord and satisfaction defense to the flood event claim (Count IV): Court of Federal Claims' analysis of the meeting of the minds was legally erroneous, so the defense was vacated and remanded for further review.
We find the Court of Federal Claims provided insufficient analysis of this defense.
6074: Unpaid contract quantities claim (Count VI) and Government set-off: the court clearly erred in dismissing the claim without analyzing the conflicting cost estimates, so it was remanded.

Therefore, we find the Court of Federal Claims clearly erred in dismissing Meridian’s unpaid contract quantities claim, in light of the conflicting information contained in the Second Amended Complaint and Mr. Weathers’s testimony.
6075: Interest accrual start date on the CDA claim: the court held accrual began on the date the contracting officer received the claim (January 7, 2011), not January 7, 2014, so the interest calculation was reversed and remanded.
6633: Reasonableness of KBR's delay-related equitable adjustment costs (idle truck costs paid to subcontractor); court held KBR failed to show the costs were reasonable and did not reach whether the government breached the force protection clause.
We conclude that the Board's determination that KBR had failed to demonstrate that its delay costs were reasonable was supported by substantial evidence.
6634: Reasonableness of KBR's double-handling and related costs claimed for the laydown yard and repairs; court held KBR failed to prove reasonableness.
Under these circumstances, we conclude that the Board did not err in finding that KBR had failed to prove the reasonableness of its double-handling costs.
6635: Whether the jury verdict method could bypass the FAR Part 31 reasonableness requirement for recovery; court held it could not.
We affirm the Board's holding that "[t]he jury verdict method does not relieve KBR from FAR Part 31's limitation of its recovery to costs that are reasonable."
6642: Contractor's prior material breach defense excusing noncompliance with PSC prohibition and entitlement to recover withheld payments
the Army's prior material breach excused KBR's noncompliance with that prohibition.
6774: Contractor's burden to identify specific improperly rejected items before the burden of justifying rejections shifts to the government; the court held the burden did not shift, favoring the government.

Because Avant did not even point to the particular items within the 2,255 rejected test items that it regarded as improperly rejected, the Board properly held that the burden of justifying the rejections did not shift to the government.
6821: Constructive change to the contract requiring contractor to perform wetland delineation at waste sites, entitling contractor to an equitable adjustment (liability; damages amount left for remand).
The FHA therefore effected a constructive contract change when it required Kiewit to perform wetland delineation at the government-designated waste sites.
7290: Causation and recoverable amount of lost salary damages for breach of the EEO settlement agreement; the court held the complaint plausibly alleged the breaches caused lost salary, reversing dismissal.
We conclude that Mr. Oliva has alleged facts sufficient to support his lost salary claim.
7607: Government's prior material breach defense: the court held DLA did not waive its prior material breach defense, which defeats the contractor's claims.
DLA cannot have waived its defense prior to Supreme's December 2014 guilty plea because it did not have a known right until Supreme finally entered that guilty plea
7608: Entitlement to CDA interest on amounts the government over-withheld: the court held a contractor must prevail on its own claim to recover CDA interest, so Supreme's prior material breach bars interest.
a contractor must be successful on its own claim to be entitled to interest under the CDA.
8612: Quantum: recoverability of post-November 30, 2015 remediation costs and CSA interest through final payment under 41 U.S.C. § 106(f); court affirmed award.

the Oil Companies were entitled to indemnification for remediation costs incurred at the McColl site from November 30, 2015 through September 30, 2019, plus interest on such costs, accruing through the date of final payment
8712: Government's argument that its payments to the unlisted CZ account were an immaterial noncompliance (no breach) was rejected; court held the government's breach was material.
We conclude that the government's breach was material because the FAR clause serves an important purpose for both parties.
8713: Government's alternative affirmative defense of payment (misdirected payments benefitted Aspen) was not resolved on appeal; remanded to the Board to decide in the first instance whether Aspen benefitted.
The question whether Aspen benefitted from the misdirected payments "is necessarily a fact-intensive task" that the Board must address in the first instance.
8909: Government's defense that EEOC and Army regulations make oral settlement agreements unenforceable was rejected; regulations are housekeeping rules that do not invalidate noncompliant agreements.
both regulations are best interpreted as housekeeping rules that do not invalidate non-compliant agreements.
9098: Quantum, equitable adjustment and time extension: GSC not entitled to a time extension for the UFC oversight because its own design coordination failure caused the delay.
But the Army's oversight, although unfortunate, did not entitle GSC to a time extension.
9345: Contract defenses and recovery: whether the government's unilateral deductions from invoices for hours not worked were a breach, i.e., whether the contractor was owed the fixed monthly amount.
The government therefore did not breach the contract when it inspected Pacific Coast's invoices and deducted payment for hours not actually provided.
9364: Quantum: recoverable damages for unexercised option years; even if bad-faith termination occurred, recovery limited to the $1,702 owed for the base year.

We see no error in the Board's analysis and its conclusion that, even if she had been terminated in bad faith, Kurkjian would not be entitled to recovery beyond what she was owed for the base year on her contract.
9636: Quantum of the equitable adjustment: contractor failed to show actual increases in wages and fringe benefits beyond the amount the VA paid, so no greater adjustment was recoverable.

Mr. Stone has not shown the existence of an actual increase of more than $21,865.37 in applicable wages and fringe benefits that was made to comply with the applicable Department of Labor wage determination, as required by FAR 52.222-43.
9768: Quantum of recoverable termination costs under the termination-for-convenience clause (reasonable charges resulting from termination, costs that reasonably could have been avoided)
the Board correctly held that the cost of software maintenance for option year one was not a "reasonable charge[]" that "resulted from the termination"
9887: Parol evidence rule: whether the trial court erred by admitting the pre-negotiation memo and testimony that the government did not believe the Mole Quaywall condition was a differing site condition, given the integrated Mod. A00057. Held no violation because the evidence did not modify contract terms and the cited recitals were not operative terms.
The trial court, therefore, did not violate the parol evidence rule.
9888: Denial of Pier B differing site condition (Type I and Type II) equitable adjustment claim; NTS argued the court improperly denied it based on the design-build nature of the contract. Held the court did not rely solely on design-build status and its element-by-element analysis was not in error.
the Court of Federal Claims simply did not make a mistake on this issue here.
10223: Amount recoverable / overcharge: the government met its burden of showing Raytheon charged unallowable lobbying and corporate-development costs, so Raytheon must repay them, with remand to quantify the amount and any penalties.
We therefore conclude that the Board erred in finding that the government failed to meet its burden of showing that Raytheon charged it for unallowable costs.
10438: Implied duty of good faith and fair dealing and superior knowledge doctrine claims dismissed; contractor's claims for failure to disclose failed to state a claim (contract defenses/recovery theories for contractor)
E&I has not made out a claim that the government breached its duty of good faith and fair dealing.
10439: Reimbursement for 20 invoices: four invoices rejected as covered by fixed-price term; late-submitted invoices forfeited
We agree with the Claims Court that the government properly rejected these four invoices.
10537: Constructive change claim: whether the Air Force impliedly or expressly ordered Aeroteam to manufacture the running gears beyond contract requirements; court found Aeroteam chose the work itself.
we affirm the Claims Court's determination that the Air Force was not liable for constructively changing the contract.
10538: Cardinal change claim: whether the government effected an alteration in the work materially different from the bargain; court found no government alteration because Aeroteam chose the in-house manufacturing.
Accordingly, we affirm the Claims Court's determination that the Air Force was not liable for making a cardinal change to the contract.
10539: Commercial impracticability defense: whether performance at PDI's higher running-gear price was impracticable due to unforeseen events; court found no clear error and that the price increase was a fixed-price risk Aeroteam assumed.
Accordingly, we affirm the court's determination that it was not impracticable for Aeroteam to perform the contract.
10749: Quantum and contract defenses: the pass-through delay claims failed because of concurrent contractor-caused delay throughout the period, so the government was not the sole proximate cause of the delay; the court also treated the relay-delay claims as waived by Modification A00016.
Accordingly, the government was not the sole substantial cause of delay at any point between June 11, 2013, and December 22, 2013.
10856: Quantum and recovery for constructive change of a firm-fixed-price contract: contractor failed to prove damages resulting from the government's constructive change, so no recovery.
Pacific Coast's failure to provide any evidence to show costs incurred as a result of the government's constructive change is fatal.
10971: Quantum and contract defenses: whether the implied duty of good faith and fair dealing supports recovery of lost profits for acreage beyond the contractual minimum; rejected as a matter of law.
The implied duty of good faith and fair dealing cannot bind the Forest Service in this regard because the duty is "limited by the original bargain."
11022: Remedy: the Claims Court's permanent injunction disqualifying Torres and directing award to the remaining offeror was not an abuse of discretion.

The Claims Court did not abuse its discretion in issuing a permanent injunction disqualifying Torres and directing an award to a responsible remaining offeror in light of the unusual facts of this case and the court's authority to award equitable relief.
11105: Contract defenses/merits of implied duty of good faith claim: implied duty tethered to existing contract terms; no breach found on summary judgment because rent was paid and no new contract was formed.
But Ricchi cited no contractual term to which the implied duty attaches, and no new contract was formed.
11380: Termination-for-convenience recovery: the percentage-of-contract-price component of damages is zero because the contract price remained at zero until ACLR collected overpayments.
Since 7.5% of zero is zero, the trial court correctly held that ACLR could not prove entitlement to any compensation in the form of a "percentage of the contract price."
11381: Settlement costs: legal fees and claim-prosecution costs are not recoverable absent a waiver of sovereign immunity, and post-March 2020 settlement costs were not shown to be reasonable charges because ACLR failed to segregate them.
recoverable settlement expenses cannot include legal fees or other charges associated with ACLR's pressing of a claim against the United States
11382: Record-keeping requirement: ACLR's records did not show a standard record keeping system under FAR 52.212-4(l), so its recoverable charges were not established.
we agree with the Court of Federal Claims that no reasonable factfinder could view ACLR's record keeping system as regularly used, carefully thought-out, or even organized and orderly.
12008: Quantum and contract defenses: whether the government may offset its partial-breach damages for Standard Contract SNF costs by investment gains on the Yankees' nuclear decommissioning trusts (mitigation and direct-relation analysis); held no offset, so damages stand for the contractor.

Because no such reduction or avoidance of loss has been shown here, we conclude that the NDTs’ investment gains do not constitute a “mitigation activity” and, therefore, cannot be credited against the damages owed by the government for its breach of contract.
12359: Constructive acceleration claim: the Board found no excusable delay (critical path not shown, no expert analysis), so the contractor failed to establish the first element; the court rejected the presumption from time extensions and affirmed.

We conclude that the Board appropriately credited the Navy's expert's testimony and substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that AGJV failed to prove excusable delay and therefore failed to establish a constructive acceleration claim.
12489: Contract defenses: prior bilateral modifications and releases barred recovery on Count I and the relevant portions of Count II.
We therefore agree with the Board's conclusion that the prior bilateral contract modifications and releases barred Count I and the relevant portions of Count II.
13005: Whether the Air Force breached the February 2014 agreement; no genuine dispute of material fact that the Air Force breached, so summary judgment for the government was proper.
Thus, the Claims Court properly granted the government's summary judgment motion, as Fox failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact that the Air Force breached.
13308: Quantum, equitable adjustment and contract defenses: whether VA's conduct (information gathering) modified the contract or excused Sergent's delay
We conclude that no assertion that the Contract was modified survives summary judgment.
13383: Enforceability of the Drag agreement against the Government: the contracting officer lacked actual authority because the advance agreement did not comply with FAR 31.109, so the agreement cannot be enforced against the Government.
Because the contracting officer lacked authority to bind the government, the Drag agreement cannot be enforced against it.
13488: Contract defense: Flatland's removal and restoration obligation under lease section 12 was excused by the Corps' prior material breach, so the Board erred in denying recovery for the building; reversed and remanded for valuation of the building.

We agree with Flatland. When the Corps breached the contract, Flatland was excused from performing the removal and restoration provision of section 12 of the lease pursuant to the common law rule of prior material breach.
13489: Quantum: Board's reduction of the concession-business damages from $360,000 to $210,000 was supported by substantial evidence; award affirmed.
We therefore affirm the part of the Board’s decision that awarded Flatland $210,000 in damages for the loss of the concession business.
13565: Damages award for breach of the 2003 Memorandum of Understanding, vacated along with the liability ruling and remanded for consideration consistent with the opinion.
we vacate the Court of Federal Claims' decision as it relates to the 2003 Memorandum of Understanding, as well as its award of damages, and remand for consideration consistent with this opinion.
13567: Damages for breach of the 2011 Memorandum of Agreement, the $11,279,059 award, which the court affirmed (while noting it is more correctly categorized as reliance damages).
as well as the trial court's award of $11,279,059 in damages to Anchorage.
13710: Contract defense/quantum: contractor's theory that the government had a duty to conduct adequate market research and that the contract was flawed from the start was rejected
We are aware of none, and this argument is without merit.
13711: Good-faith conduct of DeCA in weekly price reviews: Board's finding that DeCA acted reasonably and that MPG's losses resulted from its failure to implement a local sourcing plan was affirmed
We see no error in that fact finding with respect to almost all of the FF&V products.
13756: Quantum, equitable adjustment, contract defenses: contractor's claim for equitable adjustment denied because Spearin warranty did not apply; government recovery of improperly issued funds ($418,406) upheld
On summary judgment, the Board denied Sheffield's request for an equitable adjustment and ordered it to repay the Corps.
13819: Contract defense of excusable delay under FAR 52.212-4(f): the contractors failed to raise a genuine dispute that pandemic-related delays were excusable.
Therefore, the Court of Federal Claims did not err in finding the delays by AME, Servant, and Transcendence were not excusable.
13896: Whether HUD's diversion of inventory to REO alternatives breached the Bridge Contract (requirements/superior knowledge recovery)
Thus, HUD plainly discharged its obligation under the terms of the contract.
13959: Contract defenses and personal services challenge: contract not an unlawful personal services contract under FAR 37.104; contractor-employee supervision left with ASG.
The Claims Court was thus clearly correct that the contract was not a personal services contract.
14004: Timesheet alteration claim barred by the settlement release of all claims arising before the effective date
Mr. Strong's timesheet alteration claim therefore cannot form the basis of a valid complaint against the agency.
14058: Contract defense of waiver: Hahnenkamm as a matter of law could not reasonably rely on the independence representation because it knew of the Forest Service reviewer's involvement in the appraisal.

Because Hahnenkamm was aware of the Forest Service’s involvement with the Doré appraisal, as a matter of law, Hahnenkamm could not have reasonably relied on the representation that the appraisal was independent in this respect.
14059: Contract defense of waiver (reasonable reliance) on the Yellow Book-compliance representation: the court held this cannot be decided as a matter of law and remanded for further factfinding under the three-part test.
We do not think that the question of reliance and reasonable reliance on Yellow Book-compliance can be decided as a matter of law on this appeal.
14060: Contract defense of equitable estoppel: the court expressed no opinion on the merits and remanded for the Claims Court to decide whether an implied representation by Hahnenkamm supports estoppel.

we remand to the Claims Court to decide whether there is a basis for equitable estoppel based on an implied representation by Hahnenkamm that it viewed the appraisal as Yellow Book-compliant and would not further challenge the appraisal.
14061: Quantum of damages: the Claims Court did not abuse its discretion in refusing to treat the Cave Rock Summit property as a trophy property warranting an extraordinary premium, and in its highest-and-best-use and comparable analysis.
Designating a property as a “trophy property” does not on its face engender an additional premium attached to its value under the Yellow Book guidelines.
14410: Impossibility defense raised by the contractor against the specification's chilled water requirement was rejected.
Impossibility does not, therefore, excuse Korte's decision to ignore the demand in the specification and the drawings.
14782: Contract defenses/recovery: breach of the implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing based on pre-award conduct could not support recovery because no contract existed for CLDJ or Souda Bay. Claim rejected for government.
As we have previously made clear, however, the covenant does not attach in the absence of an underlying contract.
14783: Superior knowledge doctrine: claim rejected because the Navy's CLDJ and Souda Bay procurement actions could not have affected performance of the awarded contract, which covered only Naples, Rota and Sigonella.

the Navy's actions related to the procurement processes at CLDJ and Souda Bay could not have affected Siemens' performance under the awarded contract because that contract only encompassed work at Naples, Rota, and Sigonella.
14825: Recoverability of roughly $36 million in tax payments as reimbursable incurred costs under FAR Part 31; Board's finding that the taxes were incurred by IDS's higher-tier parents, not IDS, affirmed, so IDS not entitled to reimbursement.
Therefore, substantial evidence supports the Board's determination that the taxes paid were costs incurred by entities higher in IDS's ownership chain, rather than by IDS.
15030: Contract defenses: contractual immunity under Articles 13(b) and 19(a) of the Friant Contract for allocation decisions that were not arbitrary, capricious, or unreasonable.
Accordingly, the Court of Federal Claims was right to grant summary judgment to the government on the Friant Contractors' breach of contract claim
15346: Constructive change to the contract under the FAR 52.243-4 Changes Clause: whether Walsh plausibly pleaded a compensable constructive change entitling it to an equitable adjustment from the government's COVID-19 vaccine mandate actions, reversing the Board's dismissal.

Because Walsh's complaint sufficiently alleges a constructive change, we reverse and remand for further proceedings, including full analysis of the government's sovereign-acts-doctrine defense, which the Board did not address.
